explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul tells them, "Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them." (Colossians 3:19) Love them, and don't be harsh. It's a short instruction, but I think it takes a whole lifetime to practice.

Paul does say it, friend. His words are "Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them." (Colossians 3:19) So the husbands get a command to love and a command to be gentle, both in one verse. Easy to read, and I think harder to live, so no shame in a second look.

explanations.answer: It is pleasing to the Lord
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, "Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord." (Colossians 3:20) His reason is the Lord's pleasure, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: It brings them a long life
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, friend, but Paul doesn't say it here. He gives the reason right in the verse: "…for this is pleasing to the Lord." (Colossians 3:20) Nothing in these words promises a long life. The reason he gives is that it pleases the Lord.

explanations.answer: It keeps the home at peace
explanations.explanation: A peaceful home sounds lovely, baker, and I'd sign up for one. But that's not the reason Paul gives. He says children should obey "…for this is pleasing to the Lord." (Colossians 3:20) The text gives the Lord's pleasure as the reason.

Right on, baker. Paul says, "Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged." (Colossians 3:21) So he tells fathers not to provoke, and he names what's at stake: discouraged children. I think this one is a gentle word, and I know a little about how heavy discouragement feels after my years in that dark drawer.

Paul really does say it, friend. The verse reads, "Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged." (Colossians 3:21) The warning is for fathers, and the worry is discouraged children. So this statement matches the text.

That's it, baker. Paul says to obey "…not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord." (Colossians 3:22) The point is a heart that stays the same whether anyone is looking or not. Every grown-up knows that pull.

explanations.answer: When the masters give a reward
explanations.explanation: Close to the idea, friend, but rewards aren't what Paul names. He says "…not only to please them while they are watching…" (Colossians 3:22) The time he mentions is when the masters are watching. He wants obedience from a sincere heart, not just when someone's eyes are on them.

explanations.answer: When the masters are in a good mood
explanations.explanation: Moods don't come up in this verse, baker. What Paul says is "…not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord." (Colossians 3:22) The time he names is when the masters are watching. He wants obedience from a sincere heart either way.

Yes, baker. Paul wants obedience "…with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord." (Colossians 3:22) Sincerity means the heart matches what the hands are doing. It's like a cookie that's the same all the way through, not just frosted on top.

Good try, friend, because "hardness of heart" sounds like something you'd hear in a sermon. But Paul wants "…sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord." (Colossians 3:22) Hardness is a rock-solid cookie, and nobody wants to bite that. Sincerity is the word he picks.

Heaviness sounds like carrying a big sack of flour up the stairs, baker. Paul's word is different. He wants obedience "…with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord." (Colossians 3:22) A sincere heart is honest through and through.

That's the one, baker! Paul says, "…you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward." (Colossians 3:24) An INHERITANCE. Not a pat on the back, not a coupon that expired in 2009, but an inheritance, and it comes from the Lord Himself.

A crown sounds fancy, friend, and I'd wear it over my chef's hat. But it's not what Paul names here. He says, "…you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward." (Colossians 3:24) The reward in this verse is an inheritance.

A new name is a nice thought, baker, but Paul doesn't say it here. The verse reads, "…you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward." (Colossians 3:24) I'm pretty attached to my own name, since the Millers carved it right on my handle. The reward Paul names is an inheritance.

Let's look again, baker, because Paul says the opposite. He writes, "It is the Lord Christ you are serving." (Colossians 3:24) So the one they are really serving is the Lord Christ. Their earthly masters aren't named as the one they serve in the end.
You got it, friend. Paul says, "It is the Lord Christ you are serving." (Colossians 3:24) So the service ends up with the Lord Christ. That changes how everyday work looks.

Not quite, baker, because Paul says the opposite. The verse reads, "Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism." (Colossians 3:25) That means nobody gets special treatment. Nobody gets a pass, no matter who they are.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism." (Colossians 3:25) Nobody gets special treatment, and nobody skips the line. That includes everybody in the house.

That's right, friend. Paul says, "Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven." (Colossians 4:1) The masters answer to a Master too. Right and fair is how he says they should treat the people under them.

I get why firm came to mind, baker, since it sounds like a responsible word. But it isn't what Paul says. The verse says, "Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair…" (Colossians 4:1) Firm is for cookie dough. Paul's word is fair.

Strict is a sensible guess, friend, but it isn't Paul's word. He tells masters to supply their slaves with "…what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven." (Colossians 4:1) The word he picks is fair. They're answering to a Master of their own.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful…" (Colossians 4:2) So prayer comes with watching and thanking. I thank God every day for reaching into that drawer and calling me out, so this one's close to my heart.

Silent is a fair guess, friend, since some people picture prayer as very quiet. But Paul doesn't say it. He writes, "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful…" (Colossians 4:2) The word he picks is thankful.

Prayer can come with tears, baker, but that's not what Paul says here. He tells them, "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful…" (Colossians 4:2) The word in the verse is thankful. So gratitude goes right into the prayer.

That's it, baker. Paul asks them to pray "…that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ…" (Colossians 4:3) He's in chains, and he asks for a door for the word. I think that tells you what matters most to him.

Fair guess, friend. A door and chains go together in the mind. But Paul asks them to pray "…that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ…" (Colossians 4:3) The door he names is for the word. He doesn't ask here for the prison doors to open.

Wanting to go home is a very human thing, baker. But Paul doesn't ask for it in this verse. He asks them to pray "…that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ…" (Colossians 4:3) What he asks for is a door for the word.

You got it, baker. Paul says he wants to proclaim the mystery of Christ, "…for which I am in chains." (Colossians 4:3) The mystery of Christ is the reason for the chains. And he still asks for prayer to proclaim it.

Paul says it himself, friend. He wants to proclaim the mystery of Christ, "…for which I am in chains." (Colossians 4:3) The chains are tied to the mystery of Christ, right there in the text. And look at what he asks for while he's chained: prayer for a door to open for the word. That man is locked up and still asking for DOORS.

Let's look again, baker, because Paul says nearly the opposite. He writes, "Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time." (Colossians 4:5) He tells them to act wisely toward outsiders, not to avoid them. So the believers are told to deal with outsiders wisely.
That's right, friend. Paul says, "Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time." (Colossians 4:5) Nothing there says to avoid anyone. He wants them to act wisely when they're around outsiders.

explanations.answer: So they know how to answer everyone
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone." (Colossians 4:6) Gracious words go with knowing how to answer. And he says everyone, not just the easy people.

explanations.answer: So they can win every argument
explanations.explanation: That would be a handy skill, friend, but it isn't what Paul says. The verse reads, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone." (Colossians 4:6) The goal is knowing how to answer everyone. Winning isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: So people will speak well of them
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, baker. Everybody likes a good reputation, and I'd love a five-star review on my cookies too. But that's not what Paul says. He writes, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone." (Colossians 4:6) The reason in the verse is knowing how to answer everyone, and that has nothing to do with who's clapping.
